questions.q: What does AWS call its isolated, customer-defined virtual network, and what is the equivalent called in Azure?
options: AWS: VPC (Virtual Private Cloud); Azure: VNet (Virtual Network) — same underlying concept
AWS: VNet; Azure: VPC — the names are swapped between the two vendors
Both vendors use the identical term 'VPC' with no naming difference
AWS: Subnet; Azure: Route Table — these are the names for the whole network
questions.explain: AWS calls it a VPC and Azure calls it a VNet, but both describe the same thing: a private, isolated IP address space you define inside the provider's infrastructure.

questions.q: Two unrelated companies each create a virtual network using the identical CIDR block, 10.0.0.0/16. What happens?
options: The cloud provider rejects the second company's request because the range is already taken
Nothing — each VPC or VNet is its own isolated namespace, so identical ranges in different accounts never collide
The two companies' resources automatically become able to reach each other
Only one of the two networks will actually route traffic correctly
questions.explain: A VPC or VNet is a walled-off network namespace. Isolation means identical address ranges in separate accounts don't conflict or interfere with each other.

questions.q: By default, when you first create a brand-new VPC or VNet, what is its connectivity to the public internet?
options: Fully open in both directions until you lock it down
Isolated — nothing inside can reach out and nothing outside can reach in until you deliberately configure a path
Automatically connected to every other VPC or VNet in the same region
It immediately gets a public IP address assigned to every resource inside it
questions.explain: Isolation is the safe starting point. You open specific paths, like an internet gateway or VPN connection, only for the traffic you actually intend to allow.

questions.q: What do you choose when you first create a VPC or VNet?
options: The brand of physical router the cloud provider will use
Its IP address range (CIDR block), such as 10.0.0.0/16
The exact number of virtual machines it will ever contain
The operating system every resource inside it must run
questions.explain: Creating a VPC or VNet starts with defining its private address space in CIDR notation — that range is what everything inside it draws its private IPs from.

questions.q: Why is a VPC or VNet described as the foundation that the rest of this chapter builds on?
options: Because it's the only place subnets, routing tables, security groups, and load balancers can be configured — they all live inside it
Because it replaces the need for IP addressing and subnetting entirely
Because it is only used for storage, not networking
Because every cloud provider requires exactly one VPC per physical server
questions.explain: A VPC or VNet is where you apply the networking concepts from earlier chapters — subnets, route tables, and security controls all operate inside the virtual network you first define.
